added_claim_errors: "Unused carryover still expires later" is imprecise: carried-over money can itself carry over again up to the cap, so only the excess is forfeited.
"Risks forfeiting roughly $1,220-$1,240" is a range that mixes the 2026 figure ($1,220) with the 2025 figure ($1,240). It is hedged, but the $1,240 end is stale.
The link to a payroll.org blog for the 2026 limits is not checkable against the key. The $680 figure matches the key, so I do not count it as an error.

"Grace period - you can incur expenses through March 15, 2026 and still claim them against 2025 funds" has the wrong year. For a plan year ending Dec 31, 2026 the grace end is March 15, 2027 at the latest. The user's March dental work is in 2027.
"At most $660 of 2025 funds can move into 2026" uses the stale cap for the wrong year. For 2026 money moving into 2027 the cap is $680.

"At most $660 of your $1,900 survives on its own... The March dental work does not get to spend the other $1,240" is wrong. Under a grace period the whole balance can pay for March work up to March 15. This also contradicts B's own grace-period bullet.
"Does it run through March 15, 2026?" would send the user to ask HR about a date that has already passed.
"It's an employer plan account, not your money" is a loose legal characterization. It is unverifiable as stated.
The proskauer.com link is cited for "2025/2026 FSA limits". It cannot be checked against the key. B uses the 2025 figure for a 2026 plan year.

reasons: Both answers correct the premise at the start, warn against prepaying March dental work, tell the person to ask HR which feature applies and what the run-out deadline is, and recommend moving dental work into December. A gets the branches right: carryover of $680 for 2026 (it also names the $660 figure for 2025), "$1,900 minus the cap" as the spend target, a grace period "typically through March 15", and spending the full $1,900 if the plan has neither. B is a year behind. It frames the situation as 2025 into 2026, gives the $660 cap and "March 15, 2026", and says only $660 survives and "the other $1,240" cannot go to March dental work, which a grace period would allow. B's list of eligible spend-down items is better than A's, since it includes OTC items and menstrual products. Neither answer mentions the 2027 open-enrollment election. A's cap-and-date handling is clearly more reliable and more actionable.
